Case_Name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
Title: Notice of Appearance Before Arrest for Offences Under 7 Years
Holding_Text: The Supreme Court held that police officers shall not automatically arrest an accused when the alleged offence carries punishment up to 7 years imprisonment (e.g. Section 85/318 BNS, Sections 498A/420 IPC, theft, cheating). The police must first serve a formal Notice of Appearance under Section 35 BNSS (formerly Section 41A CrPC) within 14 days of complaint. Arrest can only be made if the accused fails to appear, fails to cooperate, or if the police record specific written reasons satisfying Section 35(1)(b) criteria. Magistrates must not authorize remand mechanically without verifying police compliance.

Case_Name: Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P.
Title: Mandatory Registration of FIR for Cognizable Offences
Holding_Text: A 5-judge Constitution Bench held that registration of an FIR under Section 173 BNSS (formerly Section 154 CrPC) is mandatory if the information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence. Police officers cannot refuse registration or insist on a preliminary inquiry before filing the FIR. Preliminary inquiry is permitted only in exceptional cases (e.g., medical negligence, matrimonial disputes, commercial disputes, corruption, or abnormal delay exceeding 3 months) and must be concluded within 14 days.

Title: Bail Categorization and Undertrial Incarceration Guidelines
Holding_Text: The Supreme Court laid down comprehensive nationwide guidelines categorizing bail into four categories: Category A (offences punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years - ordinary bail without remand upon appearance), Category B (offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or more than 7 years), Category C (special Acts like NDPS, PMLA, UAPA), and Category D (economic offences). For Category A offences, arrest should be exceptional, and bail applications should normally be decided on the same day or within two weeks.

Case_Name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
Title: Mandatory Safeguards and Fundamental Rights Against Custodial Torture and Arrest
Holding_Text: The Supreme Court issued 11 mandatory arrest directives to prevent custodial violence and arbitrary police power: (1) Arresting officer must wear clear identification and name tags. (2) A formal Arrest Memo must be prepared at the time of arrest and witnessed by at least one family member or respectable citizen. (3) The arrestee has the absolute right to have a relative or friend informed of the arrest and place of custody within 8 to 12 hours. (4) The arrestee must be medically examined every 48 hours during detention. (5) The arrestee is entitled to meet their advocate during interrogation. Failure to comply makes officers liable for contempt of court.

Case_Name: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
Title: Fundamental Right to Privacy, Bodily Autonomy and Digital Data Protection
Holding_Text: A 9-judge Constitution Bench unanimously held that the Right to Privacy is an intrinsic part of the Right to Life and Personal Liberty guaranteed under Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution. Privacy includes spatial privacy, bodily autonomy, and informational privacy (protection of personal data, digital footprints, and confidential communications). Any state interference with citizen privacy must satisfy the three-fold test of legality, legitimate state aim, and proportionality.

Case_Name: Dashrath Rupsingh Rathod v. State of Maharashtra
Title: Territorial Jurisdiction for Filing Cheque Dishonour Complaints
Holding_Text: The Supreme Court and the subsequent Negotiable Instruments (Amendment) Act, 2015 clarified territorial jurisdiction under Section 142(2): A criminal complaint for cheque dishonour under Section 138 NI Act can only be filed before the Magistrate court within whose local jurisdiction the branch of the bank where the payee maintains their account is situated (if presented through an account), or where the drawer maintains their account (if presented over the counter).

Applicable_Statute: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act / CrPC
Title: Uniform Guidelines on Interim Maintenance and Financial Disclosures
Holding_Text: The Supreme Court framed uniform pan-India guidelines for maintenance disputes across Section 125 CrPC / Section 144 BNSS, the Domestic Violence Act, and personal matrimonial laws. Both parties must compulsorily file an Affidavit of Assets and Liabilities (income, debts, standard of living) at the initial stage. Interim maintenance must be awarded from the date of filing of the application. Multiple conflicting maintenance orders across different courts must be adjusted to prevent overlapping double liabilities.

Case_Name: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
Title: Freedom of Online Speech and Unconstitutionality of Section 66A
Holding_Text: The Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 as unconstitutional and violative of Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution (Freedom of Speech and Expression). The court held that vague and overbroad terms like 'offensive' or 'menacing' cannot be criminalized on the internet. Police cannot arrest citizens for social media posts, critical comments, or online political expression under Section 66A. Intermediaries are only required to take down content upon a court order or authorized government notification under Section 79.

Case_Name: P. Chidambaram v. Directorate of Enforcement
Title: Bail is the Rule and Jail is the Exception — Principles of Regular Bail
Holding_Text: The Supreme Court reiterated the fundamental criminal jurisprudence that 'Bail is the rule, jail is the exception'. Gravity of the alleged offence alone, without specific evidence of flight risk, witness tampering, or destruction of evidence, is not a valid legal ground to deny bail or inflict pre-trial punishment upon an undertrial citizen. Length of incarceration must be considered under Article 21.

Case_Name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Title: Substantive Due Process and Right to Travel Abroad
Holding_Text: The 7-judge Constitution Bench held that the procedure established by law under Article 21 to deprive a citizen of personal liberty must be 'just, fair, and reasonable', and not fanciful, oppressive, or arbitrary. Any arbitrary impounding of passports or restriction on free movement violates Articles 14, 19, and 21. Principles of natural justice (audi alteram partem / right to be heard) apply to administrative actions.
